description.en: The band standard biceps curl is the classic two-arm bicep curl performed with a resistance band. Standing on the middle of the band with each end gripped, you curl both ends up to shoulder height. The bands provide constant tension that increases as they stretch, building bicep size with no weights.

en: Stand on the middle of a resistance band with feet shoulder-width apart.
Grip the band ends in each hand with palms facing forward.
Allow the bands to be taut at thigh level with arms extended.
Brace your core and pin your elbows against your sides.
Curl both band ends up by bending only at the elbows.
Continue until your hands reach shoulder height.
Squeeze the biceps hard at the top.
Lower the bands back down with control to full extension.
Classic bicep curl with bands
Constant band tension through the range
Useful for home training
Builds bicep size and strength
Easy to scale by changing band tension
Strong forearm engagement

description.en: The barbell lying close grip overhand row on rack is an inverted style row using a barbell set in a power rack. The close overhand grip targets the upper back and lats with no compression on the lower back.

en: Set a barbell in a rack at about waist height.
Lie underneath the bar and grip it with a close overhand grip.
Plant your feet on the floor with knees bent or legs straight.
Hang from the bar with arms fully extended and body straight.
Brace the core and squeeze the glutes to keep the body rigid.
Pull the chest up to the bar by driving the elbows down and back.
Squeeze the upper back at the top for a brief pause.
Lower yourself slowly back to full arm extension and repeat.
Builds upper back and lat strength with no spinal compression.
Close overhand grip emphasizes the rhomboids and rear delts.
Engages the biceps and forearms through the pull.
Easy to scale by adjusting the bar height.
Excellent assistance work for pull ups and rows.
Trains horizontal pulling with full bodyweight resistance.

description.en: The barbell overhead carry locks out a barbell overhead with both arms and walks for distance. It builds bilateral overhead stability, core bracing, and shoulder endurance. The barbell demands symmetric pressing strength and is harder to stabilize than dumbbells or kettlebells.

en: Press or jerk a barbell overhead to lockout. Arms fully extended.
Set feet hip-width apart. Brace your core hard.
Walk forward with controlled strides.
Keep the bar directly above your midfoot. Do not let it drift forward or back.
Maintain lockout throughout — if your elbows bend, the weight is too heavy.
Walk for 30 to 60 seconds or a set distance.
Lower the bar with control when finished.
Use moderate weight. Start light and progress slowly.
Builds bilateral overhead stability
Develops core bracing under overhead load
Trains shoulder endurance
Barbell demands symmetric strength
Useful for overhead athletes and lifters
Tests total-body stability

description.en: The barbell seated behind head military press is the classic strict press performed seated. The bar starts and finishes behind the neck at each rep, requiring excellent shoulder mobility. The seated position eliminates leg drive for strict pressing strength. It is an old-school bodybuilding favorite for shoulder mass.

en: Sit on a bench with a vertical back support.
Position the barbell across your rear delts at the base of the neck.
Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width.
Sit tall with chest up and core braced.
Press the bar straight overhead by extending your arms.
Continue until your elbows lock out at the top.
Lower the bar back down behind your neck with control.
Stop just before the bar touches your traps.
Strict overhead pressing strength
Builds shoulder mass
Old-school bodybuilding favorite
No leg drive contribution
Develops shoulder mobility
Strong stimulus for the side delts

description.en: The barbell seated shrug performs shrugs while seated on a bench, eliminating leg drive and body english for strict upper trap isolation. The seated position makes cheating impossible, ensuring every rep is pure trap work.

en: Sit on a flat bench. Hold a barbell at arm’s length in front of your thighs with an overhand grip.
Sit tall. Pull your shoulders back.
Shrug your shoulders straight up toward your ears.
Squeeze your upper traps hard at the top. Hold for one to two seconds.
Lower under control.
Keep your arms straight — only your shoulders move.
Seated position eliminates all momentum.
Use moderate weight. Aim for 12 to 15 reps.
Strict trap isolation from seated position
Eliminates leg drive and momentum
Easy to load progressively
Builds upper trap thickness
Simple setup
Useful when standing shrugs involve too much body english

description.en: Battling ropes (battle ropes) are heavy, thick training ropes anchored to a fixed point. You hold one end in each hand and generate waves by rapidly moving your arms up and down (or in other patterns). They provide intense full-body conditioning with minimal joint stress, making them a staple in functional training and conditioning.

en: Anchor a battle rope to a sturdy fixed point. Walk back so the rope is taut with slight slack.
Grip one end of the rope in each hand with a firm grip.
Stand with feet shoulder-width apart in a quarter-squat athletic stance.
Brace your core. Pull your shoulders back and down.
Begin rapidly moving both arms up and down, generating waves down the rope.
Keep the waves consistent. Move your arms quickly with full range.
For variations: alternate single-arm waves, slams (both arms slam down), or in/out waves.
Perform for 15 to 30 seconds per interval. Rest fully between intervals.
Intense full-body conditioning
Builds shoulder endurance
Burns calories at a very high rate
Low joint stress despite high intensity
Excellent metabolic conditioning
Time-efficient HIIT exercise

description.en: The bodyweight step up on stepbox is a simple lower body conditioning move using a low step platform. Alternating step ups build leg endurance, balance, and cardiovascular fitness.

en: Stand facing a sturdy step box or low platform.
Place one foot fully flat on top of the box.
Drive through the front heel to step up onto the box.
Stand tall with both feet on the box at the top.
Step the same foot back down to the floor.
Step the other foot down to return to the start.
Repeat with the opposite leg leading the next step up.
Continue alternating sides for the full set.
Builds leg endurance and single leg strength.
Improves balance and coordination.
Joint friendly low impact lower body cardio.
No equipment beyond a step box.
Develops carryover to walking and stair climbing.
Easy to scale by increasing tempo or step height.

description.en: The cable lying triceps extension II is performed on a flat bench positioned in front of a low cable pulley. A rope or bar attachment is taken behind the head, and the elbows extend to lock out. The cable provides constant tension throughout the rep, unlike a barbell or dumbbell.

en: Set a flat bench in front of a low cable pulley.
Attach a rope or straight bar to the cable.
Lie back on the bench with your head near the cable.
Reach overhead and grab the attachment.
Start with arms extended above your forehead.
Bend at the elbows to lower the attachment behind your head.
Keep your upper arms still and only the elbows moving.
Extend the elbows to return to the start position.
Constant cable tension
Stretches the long head of the triceps
Builds triceps mass
Smoother resistance than barbell
Reduces wrist strain
Strong triceps isolation

description.en: The cable one arm twisting seated row is a single-arm seated cable row that rotates the torso during the pull. The torso starts twisted toward the cable and rotates away as the handle rows back. It combines unilateral back work with rotational obliques training. It is a great functional move.

en: Sit at a cable row machine with feet on the platform.
Attach a single D-handle to the low cable.
Grab the handle with one hand.
Sit upright with a tall back.
Brace your core and keep your chest up.
Pull the handle back toward your hip while rotating your torso away from the cable.
Squeeze the lat and oblique at the end of the rep.
Return slowly to the start. Complete reps on one side before switching.
Builds rotational core strength
Trains the obliques
Strong unilateral back work
Useful for athletes
Builds back thickness
Strong functional move

description.en: The cable reverse grip pulldown is a lat pulldown variation where you grip the bar with palms facing you (underhand/supinated grip). The grip change shifts emphasis to the lower lats and increases bicep involvement compared to the standard overhand pulldown.

en: Sit at a lat pulldown machine. Grip the bar with hands shoulder-width apart using an underhand (supinated) grip — palms facing you.
Adjust the thigh pad to lock your legs in place. Lean back slightly (about 15 degrees).
Brace your core. Pull your shoulders back and down.
Pull the bar down to your upper chest by driving your elbows down and back along your sides.
Continue until the bar touches your upper chest or just below your collarbone.
Squeeze your lats and lower back hard at the bottom.
Slowly let the bar travel back up to fully extended arms over two to three seconds.
Use moderate weight — the underhand grip can stress the wrists and biceps.
Emphasizes the lower lats
Increases bicep involvement
Different stimulus than overhand pulldowns
Easier on the shoulders for some lifters
Builds lat thickness
Useful variation for back day

description.en: The captain's chair leg raise is a core exercise performed on a captain's chair (vertical knee raise station) — a piece of equipment with elbow pads and back support. With your forearms supported on the pads, you lift your knees or legs up toward your chest. The supported position eliminates grip and shoulder demand, allowing you to focus purely on the abs.

en: Step up onto the captain’s chair and place your forearms on the pads. Grip the handles firmly.
Press your back firmly against the back pad. Let your legs hang straight down.
Brace your core hard. Pull your shoulders down and away from your ears.
Lift both knees up toward your chest by contracting your abs and hip flexors. Bend at the knees and hips.
For more challenge: keep your legs straight (straight-leg raise) or curl your hips up at the top.
Continue lifting until your knees are at chest height or higher. Pause briefly and squeeze your abs.
Lower your legs slowly under control over a count of two to three seconds back to the hanging start position.
Avoid swinging or kicking. Strict reps are far more effective than sloppy momentum-driven reps.
Direct isolation of the lower abs and hip flexors
Eliminates grip and shoulder demand vs hanging variations
Excellent for high-rep ab volume work
Easier to perform strictly than hanging exercises
Allows easy progression from bent-knee to straight-leg variations
Standard equipment in most commercial gyms

description.en: The chest stretch with exercise ball is a passive chest opener done with a stability ball. Draping the upper back over the ball with the arms extended overhead lets gravity pull the chest into a deep stretch.

en: Sit on the floor in front of a stability ball.
Roll back so the upper back rests on the ball.
Walk the feet out to extend the body.
Allow the arms to fall back overhead.
Brace the core lightly and keep the hips supported.
Let the chest open into the stretch.
Breathe slowly and deeply to relax.
Hold for the desired duration.
Stretches the chest deeply.
Opens the front shoulders.
Mobilizes the thoracic spine.
Useful after pressing work.
Improves posture.

description.en: The cross-body crunch crunches with rotation, bringing opposite elbow toward opposite knee. It targets both the rectus abdominis and obliques in one movement — essentially the same as the bicycle crunch but performed one rep at a time.

en: Lie on your back, knees bent, feet flat. Hands behind head.
Crunch up and rotate — bring right elbow toward left knee.
Lower back to start.
Crunch and rotate the other way — left elbow to right knee.
Continue alternating.
Focus on the rotation and oblique contraction.
Aim for 10 to 15 reps per side.
Move with control.
Targets abs and obliques together
Cross-body pattern builds rotational strength
No equipment needed
Classic core exercise
Easy to learn
Effective for oblique development

description.en: The double jump squat is a plyometric variation where you perform two consecutive jumps before returning to the squat. The first jump is from a deep squat (high effort), the second is a smaller bounce jump from a partial squat (reactive). It builds endurance, reactive power, and ankle/calf strength.

en: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart.
Sit into a deep squat, then explode up into a high jump.
Land softly on the balls of your feet with bent knees.
Immediately bounce into a second smaller jump — this comes from a quarter-squat with quick reactive force.
Land again with bent knees.
Drop back into the deep squat and repeat the sequence (deep squat → high jump → bounce jump → repeat).
Move continuously — do not pause between the jumps.
Perform for time (20 to 45 seconds) or rounds.
Combines max-effort and reactive jumps
Builds reactive power for sports
Develops calf and ankle stiffness
Excellent cardiovascular conditioning
No equipment needed
More demanding than single jump squats

description.en: The dumbbell goblet split squat holds a dumbbell at the chest (goblet position) while performing a stationary split squat. The front-loaded position forces an upright torso, emphasizing the quadriceps on the front leg.

en: Hold a dumbbell vertically at your chest (goblet position).
Step one foot forward into a split stance.
This is your fixed position.
Lower your back knee toward the floor by bending both knees.
Descend until your back knee is just above the floor.
Drive through your front foot to stand back up.
Complete reps, then switch feet.
Keep torso upright throughout.
Front-loaded position emphasizes quads
Goblet hold keeps torso upright
Builds single-leg strength
Easy to set up
Exposes left-right imbalances
Useful for learning split squat pattern

description.en: The dumbbell good morning squat combines a hip hinge (good morning) and a squat in one fluid movement. Holding a dumbbell at your chest, you hinge forward to load the hamstrings, then drop into a squat to load the quads and glutes before standing back up. It hits the entire lower body with one rep.

en: Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart. Hold a dumbbell vertically at your chest with both hands.
Brace your core and pull your shoulders back.
Hinge at your hips, keeping your back flat, until your torso is parallel to the floor — this is the good morning position.
Pause briefly with the load on your hamstrings.
From the hinged position, bend your knees and drop into a squat without raising your torso first.
Squat down until your thighs are parallel to the floor.
Drive through your heels to stand back up to the starting position in one motion.
Aim for 8 to 12 reps. Move smoothly between positions, avoiding jerky transitions.
Trains the hip hinge and squat patterns in one exercise
Builds the entire posterior chain
Develops quad and glute strength
Time-efficient lower body movement
Great warm-up or finisher
Improves coordination of compound patterns

description.en: The dumbbell incline fly (also listed as "incline breeding" in some databases) is a chest fly performed on an incline bench targeting the upper (clavicular) pectoralis major. You arc the dumbbells out to the sides and bring them back together above your upper chest.

en: Set an incline bench to 30 to 45 degrees. Lie back with a dumbbell in each hand above your chest.
Start with arms extended above your upper chest, palms facing each other. Slight elbow bend.
Arc both dumbbells out to the sides, maintaining the elbow bend.
Lower until you feel a deep stretch across your upper chest.
Pull the dumbbells back together by squeezing your chest.
Squeeze at the top.
Use lighter weight than pressing movements.
Aim for 10 to 15 reps per set.
Targets the upper (clavicular) chest
Deep stretch at the bottom
Builds upper chest shape and definition
Isolation movement with no tricep involvement
Easy to load progressively
Classic chest exercise

description.en: The dumbbell lying external shoulder rotation is a rotator cuff exercise where you lie on your side and rotate the top arm's forearm upward against a light dumbbell. It targets the infraspinatus and teres minor — the external rotators of the shoulder — essential for shoulder health.

en: Lie on your left side on the floor or a bench.
Bend your right elbow at 90 degrees. Upper arm against your side.
Hold a light dumbbell in your right hand. Forearm starts across your stomach (pointing down).
Rotate your forearm upward, away from your body, toward the ceiling.
Rotate until your forearm is pointing straight up.
Slowly lower back to the starting position under control.
Keep your elbow pinned to your side throughout — only your forearm rotates.
Use very light weight (2 to 10 lbs). Aim for 15 to 20 reps per side.
Strengthens the external rotators (infraspinatus, teres minor)
Essential for shoulder health
Prevents shoulder injuries
Simple setup with light dumbbells
Rehabilitation and prehab exercise
Important for overhead athletes

description.en: The dumbbell one arm lunge, often called the suitcase lunge, holds a single dumbbell at one side of the body while performing forward or reverse lunges. The asymmetric load creates lateral force the core must resist. It builds single-leg strength along with anti-lateral-flexion core stability.

en: Stand with feet hip-width apart, holding a single dumbbell in your right hand at your side.
Brace your core hard against the asymmetric load.
Step forward with either leg into a forward lunge.
Lower until your front thigh is parallel to the floor and back knee approaches the floor.
Keep your shoulders square and resist tilting toward the dumbbell.
Drive through the front foot to step back to the starting position.
Complete reps with the dumbbell on one side, then switch.
Maintain a tall, level torso throughout.
Trains anti-lateral-flexion core stability
Asymmetric loading challenges trunk control
Builds single-leg strength
Strong oblique and quadratus lumborum work
Functional carryover to daily lifting
Useful for core integration with leg work

description.en: The dumbbell plyo squat adds dumbbell loading to bodyweight jump squats. You hold dumbbells at your sides, squat down, then explode upward into a jump. It builds lower-body explosive power with added resistance for more fast-twitch fiber recruitment.

en: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Hold a dumbbell in each hand at your sides.
Squat down to a partial squat (quarter to half squat).
Explode upward, jumping off the floor with maximum force.
The dumbbells stay at your sides throughout.
Land softly with bent knees. Absorb the landing.
Immediately drop into the next rep.
Use moderate weight. Too heavy compromises the jump.
Aim for 5 to 8 reps per set with maximum effort.
Adds resistance to jump squats
Builds explosive lower-body power
Develops fast-twitch fibers
Excellent for athletes
Time-efficient power exercise
Carries over to sport performance

description.en: The dumbbell push jerk uses an explosive leg dip and drive followed by a quick re-dip under the dumbbells to lock them out overhead. Unlike a push press where you press the dumbbells once they leave the shoulders, the jerk involves catching them in a partial squat with arms locked.

en: Stand with dumbbells at shoulder height in a front rack position. Feet hip-width apart.
Brace your core.
Dip slightly by bending your knees (4 to 6 inches).
Drive explosively through your legs. The dumbbells leave your shoulders.
As the dumbbells rise, dip again under them by bending your knees.
Lock out your arms overhead in the second dip.
Stand up from the second dip with the dumbbells locked overhead.
Lower to shoulders. Use moderate weight. Aim for 5 to 8 reps.
Builds explosive overhead pressing power
Allows heavier loading than push press
Develops leg drive timing
Excellent conditioning exercise
Useful CrossFit and athletic exercise
Trains catching mechanics

description.en: The dumbbell squat lunges jump complex links three lower-body movements into a single intense flow. Holding dumbbells at your sides or shoulders, you perform a squat, alternating reverse lunges, and a jump squat in sequence. The complex builds leg strength under fatigue and serious metabolic demand.

en: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand at your sides or shoulders.
Begin with a full squat, lowering until your thighs are parallel to the floor, then standing.
Step back with your right leg into a reverse lunge until your back knee nearly touches the floor.
Drive back to standing.
Step back with your left leg into a reverse lunge, then return to standing.
Drop into a quarter squat, then explode upward into a jump squat.
Land softly with bent knees back in the starting stance.
That is one round of the complex. Continue through the chain with smooth transitions.
Brutal lower-body conditioning combo
Trains squat, lunge, and jump patterns together
Builds leg strength under fatigue
Strong cardiovascular component
Time-efficient leg burner
Develops explosive power and endurance simultaneously

description.en: The dumbbell standing back wrist curl is performed standing with dumbbells held behind the body at hip level. From this position you flex and extend the wrists to curl the dumbbells through a full range. The behind-the-back position frees the wrists from the body for complete forearm flexion.

en: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart.
Hold a dumbbell in each hand behind your body with palms facing back.
Stand upright with the dumbbells resting against the back of your thighs.
Brace your core and stand tall.
Allow the dumbbells to roll down to your fingertips.
Curl the dumbbells back up by flexing your wrists.
Squeeze your forearms hard at the top of the curl.
Lower the dumbbells back down to the fingertip position with control.
Trains forearm flexors through full range
Behind-the-back position frees the wrists
Builds grip strength
Develops wrist flexion strength
Allows progressive loading
Useful for athletes who need strong forearms

description.en: The dumbbell straight-arm pullover is the classic pullover performed with arms kept as straight as possible throughout the arc. The straight arms create a longer lever, increasing lat and serratus anterior demand compared to bent-arm versions.

en: Lie on a flat bench. Hold a dumbbell above your chest with both hands, arms extended straight.
Keep your arms straight (minimal elbow bend) throughout.
Arc the dumbbell behind your head toward the floor.
Continue until you feel a deep stretch in your lats and chest.
Pull the dumbbell back over to above your chest using your lats.
Squeeze at the top.
The straight arms make this harder than bent-arm version — use lighter weight.
Aim for 10 to 12 reps.
Longer lever arm increases lat demand
Builds the lats, chest, and serratus anterior
Deep overhead stretch
Classic bodybuilding exercise
Improves shoulder flexibility
Excellent for ribcage expansion (traditional belief)

description.en: The EZ barbell curl is a bicep curl performed with an EZ curl bar, whose angled grips reduce wrist and forearm strain compared to a straight barbell. The slight wrist angle also shifts some emphasis from the biceps brachii to the brachialis and brachioradialis, making it a versatile arm builder. It is one of the most popular bicep exercises in any gym.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Grip the EZ bar on the inner angled portions with an underhand (supinated) grip. Wrap your thumbs around the bar.
Let the bar hang at arm’s length in front of your thighs. Pull your shoulders back and brace your core.
Pin your elbows against your sides. They should not move forward or backward during the lift.
Curl the bar up by bending only at the elbows, contracting your biceps hard.
Continue until the bar reaches shoulder height. Squeeze your biceps for one second at the top.
Lower the bar under control over two seconds back to the start position. Fully extend your arms.
Do not swing your torso, lean back, or use momentum.
Repeat for the desired number of reps. Adjust grip to the outer angled portions for a slightly different stimulus.
Easier on the wrists than a straight barbell curl
Builds the biceps, brachialis, and brachioradialis
Allows heavier loading than dumbbell curls
One of the most versatile arm exercises
Easy to load progressively over time
Useful for lifters with wrist discomfort on straight bars

description.en: The ez barbell spider curl is performed face-down on an incline bench with the arms hanging straight down toward the floor. An EZ bar is curled up toward the chin with no body swing whatsoever. The angled grips reduce wrist strain. It is one of the strictest biceps curls possible.

en: Set an incline bench to about 45 degrees.
Lie face-down on the bench with chest pressed against the pad.
Let your arms hang straight down toward the floor.
Hold an EZ curl bar with an underhand grip on the angled grips.
Brace your core and keep your chest pressed to the bench.
Curl the bar up toward your chin.
Squeeze the biceps hard at the top.
Lower the bar slowly back to full arm extension.
Strictest biceps curl variation
Eliminates all body swing
Reduces wrist strain
Builds biceps shape
Strong peak contraction
Useful for biceps detail

description.en: The EZ-bar seated wrist curl is a forearm flexor isolation move performed seated with the forearms resting on the thighs. The angled EZ-bar grip is wrist-friendly compared to a straight bar. Only the wrists move, isolating the forearm flexors for direct grip and forearm growth.

en: Sit on a bench with feet flat on the floor.
Hold an EZ bar with an underhand (palms-up) grip.
Rest your forearms on your thighs with wrists hanging just past the knees.
Let the bar roll down to your fingertips.
Curl your fingers and wrists up to lift the bar.
Keep your forearms pressed against your thighs.
Squeeze the forearms hard at the top.
Lower the bar slowly back to the start.
Isolates the forearm flexors
Wrist-friendly EZ bar grip
Builds grip strength
Develops forearm size
Useful for grip-intensive sports
Easy to set up and execute

description.en: The forward step front plank is a dynamic plank variation. The lifter holds a high plank and walks the hands forward one at a time while keeping the body in a straight line. The forward walk creates a brutal core challenge as the hands move further from the feet.

en: Begin in a high plank position with hands under the shoulders.
Set the body in a straight line from head to heels.
Brace your core hard.
Step one hand forward keeping the body steady.
Step the other hand forward to match.
Continue walking the hands forward step by step.
Keep the hips level and the body in a straight line throughout.
Walk the hands back to the start to finish the rep.
Brutal core builder
Trains anti-extension
Builds shoulder stability
No equipment needed
Useful core finisher
Strong functional pattern

description.en: The glute-ham raise (GHR) is a posterior chain exercise performed on a glute-ham developer (GHD) machine. You start face down with hips on the pad and knees on the knee pad, then lower your torso forward and pull yourself back up using your hamstrings and glutes. It combines knee flexion and hip extension in one movement.

en: Set up on a GHD machine. Knees on the pad, feet locked under the foot pads. Hips on the front pad.
Start upright with torso perpendicular to the floor.
Lower your torso forward by extending at the knees and hips.
Continue until your body is roughly horizontal or below.
Pull yourself back up using your hamstrings (knee flexion) and glutes (hip extension).
Return to the upright starting position.
Use slow, controlled movement. No momentum.
Aim for 6 to 10 reps per set. This is very demanding.
Combines knee flexion and hip extension in one movement
One of the best hamstring exercises available
Builds the hamstrings through full range
Develops posterior chain strength
Prevents hamstring injuries
Builds eccentric hamstring control

musclesWorked: Hamstrings (heavy — both knee flexion and hip extension)

description.en: Hands to feet pose or Pada Hastasana is a yoga forward fold with the hands tucked under the feet. The deep fold stretches the hamstrings, calves, and lower back.

en: Stand tall with feet hip width apart.
Inhale and reach the arms up overhead.
Exhale and hinge forward at the hips with a flat back.
Lower the torso toward the legs as far as comfortable.
Place the hands palms up under the soles of the feet.
The toes should rest on the inside of the wrists.
Pull gently with the arms to deepen the forward fold.
Hold the pose breathing steadily then release.
Deeply stretches the hamstrings and calves.
Opens the lower back and spine.
Improves shoulder and arm flexibility.
Calms the nervous system through the inversion.
No equipment needed.
Excellent counter to long sitting.

description.en: The hanging straight leg raise hangs from a bar and lifts both legs straight to horizontal or above without bending the knees. The straight legs create a longer lever than hanging knee raises, making it significantly harder.

en: Hang from a pull-up bar with arms extended.
Keep both legs straight.
Raise your legs in front of you to at least horizontal (90 degrees).
Control the movement — no swinging.
Lower under control. Stop before legs swing behind you.
Straight legs are much harder than bent-knee raises.
If you swing, the weight is too heavy for strict form — try bent-knee version.
Aim for 8 to 12 reps.
Advanced hanging core exercise
Straight legs increase difficulty significantly
Builds lower ab and hip flexor strength
Develops grip endurance
Progression from hanging knee raises
Builds toward toes-to-bar

description.en: The kettlebell alternating renegade row combines a plank hold with alternating single-arm rows. You hold a high plank position with hands on two kettlebells and alternately row one KB to your hip while stabilizing on the other. It builds back strength, anti-rotation core, and shoulder stability.

en: Place two kettlebells on the floor shoulder-width apart. Get into a high plank with each hand gripping a KB handle.
Set your feet wider than hip-width for stability.
Brace your core hard. Maintain a straight body line from heels to head.
Row the right KB up to your right hip by driving your elbow back.
Keep your hips perfectly still — do not rotate.
Lower the right KB to the floor under control.
Row the left KB. Continue alternating.
Use moderate weight. Aim for 8 to 12 reps per side.
Combines back rowing with core anti-rotation
Builds shoulder stability under unilateral load
Time-efficient compound exercise
Develops grip strength
Useful for full-body conditioning
Engaging challenging variation

description.en: The kettlebell extended range one arm press on floor uses an offset kettlebell to lower the elbow off a slight platform or with the arm angled, increasing the range of motion beyond a standard floor press.

en: Lie on your back on the floor with knees bent and feet flat.
Press a kettlebell up to lockout with one arm.
Extend the non working arm out wide for stability.
Brace the core and tuck the working elbow at about 45 degrees.
Lower the kettlebell slowly until the upper arm passes the floor line.
Allow the elbow to extend back for a deep chest stretch.
Press the kettlebell back up to lockout while keeping the wrist neutral.
Complete all reps on one side then switch arms.
Greater range of motion than a standard floor press.
Builds chest and triceps with deep stretch overload.
Single arm work corrects strength imbalances.
Trains shoulder stability with the offset kettlebell load.
Floor position protects the shoulder from over reaching.
Develops grip and forearm strength.

description.en: The kettlebell floor fly is performed lying on your back on the floor with a kettlebell in each hand. The floor stops the descent of the kettlebells, providing a safe and limited range of motion. The fly pattern targets the pecs while the floor protects the shoulders from over-stretching.

en: Lie on your back on the floor with knees bent and feet flat.
Hold a kettlebell in each hand pressed together over your chest.
Position the kettlebells with palms facing each other (neutral grip).
Brace your core and pull your shoulders down and back.
Maintain a slight bend in the elbows throughout.
Lower the kettlebells out to the sides in a wide arc.
Allow your upper arms to touch the floor briefly.
Squeeze your chest to bring the kettlebells back up over your chest.
Floor stops descent for shoulder safety
Builds chest size with the fly pattern
Useful for home training without a bench
Limited range protects the shoulders
Strong chest stretch within the safe range
Easy to scale by changing kettlebell weight

description.en: The kettlebell front raise is a front-delt isolation exercise where you grip a kettlebell handle with both hands (or one) and raise it straight forward to shoulder height. The kettlebell's offset weight makes this slightly different from a dumbbell front raise — the bell hangs below the handle, demanding more shoulder stabilization.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Hold a kettlebell with both hands by the handle (or one hand for unilateral).
Let the kettlebell hang at your thighs with arms extended.
Stand tall with chest lifted. Brace your core.
Raise the kettlebell straight up in front of you to shoulder height.
Keep your arms straight throughout, with just a slight bend in the elbows.
Pause briefly at shoulder height. Squeeze your front delts.
Lower under control back to your thighs over two seconds.
Use moderate weight. The kettlebell’s offset weight requires control.
Isolates the front delts
Different stimulus than dumbbell front raises
Builds shoulder stabilizer strength
Easy to scale by kettlebell weight
Useful when only kettlebells are available
Single-arm variation challenges core

description.en: The kick through push-up combines a push-up with a kick-through movement from animal flow. After each push-up, one leg kicks through under the body to the opposite side, lifting the same-side hand for balance. It builds full-body coordination, core control, and conditioning.

en: Get into a push-up position with hands under shoulders.
Brace your core and keep your body in a straight line.
Lower your chest to the floor in a controlled push-up.
Press back up to the top of the push-up.
Lift the right hand and kick the right leg under your body to the left side.
Pivot on your left foot and right hand briefly off the floor.
Return to the push-up position.
Alternate sides each rep.
Builds full-body coordination
Trains core control and stability
Combines strength and conditioning
No equipment required
Useful for athletic training
Strong calorie burner

description.en: The legs up the wall yoga pose is a restorative pose done by lying on the back with the legs vertical against a wall. The inversion helps drain the legs and decompress the lower back while gently stretching the hamstrings.

en: Sit on the floor next to a wall with one hip touching it.
Roll onto the back while swinging the legs up the wall.
Set the hips as close to the wall as comfortable.
Allow the legs to rest vertical against the wall.
Place the arms at the sides palms up.
Close the eyes and relax the body.
Breathe slowly and deeply.
Hold the pose for the desired duration.
Decompresses the lower back.
Drains fluid from the legs.
Stretches the hamstrings gently.
Calms the nervous system.
Useful for recovery.

description.en: The lying knee-to-chest stretch is a supine flexibility exercise where you lie on your back and pull one or both knees toward your chest. It is one of the simplest, most effective stretches for relieving lower back tension and stretching the glutes. It works particularly well at the end of training sessions or before bed.

en: Lie flat on your back with both legs extended on the floor.
Bend your right knee and bring it toward your chest.
Wrap both hands around your right shin or behind your right thigh.
Gently pull your knee closer to your chest until you feel a comfortable stretch.
Keep your left leg flat on the floor (or bend the left knee with foot flat for less intensity).
Hold for 20 to 30 seconds. Breathe deeply and relax.
Release and switch to the left knee.
For both knees together: pull both toward your chest simultaneously and rock gently side to side.
Relieves lower-back tension
Stretches the glutes and hip extensors
Calming and restorative
Gentle enough for daily use and rehabilitation
No equipment needed
Useful before bed for back relaxation

description.en: The lever lateral raise is a side-delt isolation exercise performed on a dedicated lateral raise machine. With your upper arms braced against padded levers, you lift the weight by abducting your arms to your sides. The guided path eliminates cheating and provides constant resistance, making it one of the strictest side-delt exercises available.

en: Adjust the seat height so that the arm pads align with the outside of your upper arms.
Sit with your back firmly against the pad and place the outsides of your upper arms against the arm pads.
Grip the handles if provided. Brace your core and pull your shoulders down.
Lift the pads out to your sides by abducting your arms. Keep your torso upright — do not lean.
Continue lifting until your upper arms are roughly parallel to the floor.
Pause briefly at the top. Squeeze your side delts.
Lower the pads under control over two to three seconds. Stop just before the weight stack touches down.
Repeat for the desired number of reps. Aim for 12 to 20 reps per set.
Strict side-delt isolation with no cheating possible
Constant resistance throughout the range of motion
Easy to load progressively in small increments
Eliminates the temptation to use momentum or body swing
Excellent for high-rep side-delt finishing work
Easier to feel the target muscle than dumbbell raises

description.en: The oblique V up on the floor is a side lying ab exercise. From the side, you lift the torso and legs together to form a V shape that hammers the obliques.

en: Lie on your side with the legs extended and stacked.
Place the bottom arm on the floor for support.
Place the top hand behind the head.
Brace the core and squeeze the obliques.
Lift the torso and legs at the same time toward each other.
Form a V shape with the body at the top.
Squeeze the obliques hard at the top.
Lower back down with control and repeat for all reps then switch sides.
Hammers the obliques in a V shape.
Builds rotational core strength.
No equipment needed.
Carryover to athletic rotation.
Improves side body strength.
Develops mind muscle connection through the obliques.

description.en: The plank jack on elbows is a dynamic plank variation that adds jumping jack feet. The lifter holds a forearm plank and hops the feet wide and back together. The forearm position adds shoulder challenge while the hops add cardio to the plank.

en: Begin in a forearm plank position.
Set the elbows under the shoulders and the body in a straight line.
Brace your core hard and keep the hips level.
Hop both feet out wide to the sides at the same time.
Land softly with feet wide.
Hop both feet back together to the start.
Continue the jumping jack feet pattern at speed.
Keep the upper body steady throughout.
Strong core and cardio combo
Trains the gluteus medius
Builds shoulder stability
No equipment needed
Useful core finisher
Builds cardio capacity

description.en: The resistance band squat with horizontal pallof hold pairs a bodyweight squat with a pallof press hold. The lifter holds the band pressed out to the side while squatting. It builds leg strength and anti-rotation core stability simultaneously.

en: Anchor a resistance band at chest height to the side.
Stand sideways to the anchor.
Hold the band handle with both hands at the chest.
Press the handle straight out to full arm extension.
Brace your core and resist the rotation.
Lower into a squat by bending the knees and hips.
Stand back up while holding the band extended.
Finish all reps then switch sides.
Trains anti-rotation core
Builds squat strength
Combo leg and core move
Strong functional drill
Useful for athletes

description.en: The resistance band standing balance glute kickback is a unilateral glute drill. Standing on one leg while pressing the other foot back against band tension isolates the glute on the working side and trains balance.

en: Anchor a resistance band at low height.
Loop the band around one ankle.
Stand facing the anchor with the working foot lifted.
Brace the core and keep the chest up.
Press the working foot straight back against the band.
Squeeze the glute hard at full extension.
Lower the foot with control without touching down.
Continue for all reps then switch sides.
Isolates the glute.
Trains balance on one leg.
Light load is joint friendly.
Useful glute activation.
Builds the glute medius for stability.

description.en: The reverse shoulder stretch is a simple standing stretch where you clasp your hands behind your back and lift them upward to open the chest, anterior shoulders, and biceps. It is one of the most effective stretches for desk workers and anyone with rounded shoulder posture.

en: Stand or sit tall with feet hip-width apart.
Reach both arms behind your back. Clasp your hands together with palms facing inward or fingers interlaced.
Pull your shoulders back and down.
Slowly lift your clasped hands up and away from your body, behind you.
Continue lifting until you feel a deep stretch across your chest, front shoulders, and biceps.
Keep your chest lifted and core braced. Avoid arching your lower back.
Hold for 20 to 30 seconds. Breathe deeply.
Release slowly and repeat two to three times.
Opens the chest, front shoulders, and biceps
Counteracts rounded shoulder posture
Quick and accessible
No equipment needed
Excellent for desk workers
Improves shoulder mobility

description.en: The roll front shoulder and chest lying on floor is a self myofascial release drill that covers the chest and front shoulder together. Lying face down with a foam roller diagonally across the upper chest and front delt releases tightness from heavy pressing and forward posture.

en: Lie face down on the floor.
Place a foam roller diagonally under the chest and front shoulder.
Extend the working arm out to the side.
Brace the body on the other forearm.
Keep the working chest and shoulder relaxed over the roller.
Roll slowly across the chest and front delt.
Pause on tender spots for several breaths.
Continue for the working time then switch sides.
Releases the chest and front shoulder.
Improves shoulder posture.
Reduces front body tightness.
Useful after pressing work.
Joint friendly release.

description.en: The rollover is a Pilates exercise where you lie on your back, lift your legs overhead until your toes touch the floor behind your head, then roll back down one vertebra at a time. It builds spinal flexibility, core control, and hamstring length. It is an intermediate-to-advanced Pilates exercise requiring neck health and spinal mobility.

en: Lie on your back with arms at your sides, palms down. Legs extended straight up toward the ceiling.
Brace your core. Press your palms into the floor for support.
Exhale and lift your hips off the floor, rolling your legs overhead toward the floor behind your head.
If your flexibility allows, touch your toes to the floor behind your head. Do not force this.
Open your legs to shoulder-width at the end position.
Slowly roll back down one vertebra at a time, controlling the descent with your abdominals.
Lower your legs back to the starting vertical position. Close your legs together.
Repeat for 3 to 5 reps. Do not perform this exercise if you have neck issues.
Builds spinal flexibility through full range
Develops core control during the roll-up and roll-down
Stretches the hamstrings and entire posterior chain
Teaches sequential spinal articulation
Foundational intermediate Pilates exercise
Decompresses the spine at the end range

description.en: The run and hop is an athletic conditioning drill where you alternate jogging strides with explosive single-leg hops for distance. It builds single-leg power, sprint mechanics, and cardiovascular conditioning. It is commonly used in track and field and team sport training.

en: Start in a jogging position. Take a few jogging steps to set rhythm.
On your right foot, push off explosively into a single-leg hop forward — drive your right knee up high.
Land on your right foot and continue jogging for two to three steps.
Push off your left foot into a single-leg hop forward — drive the left knee up high.
Continue alternating: jog → right hop → jog → left hop.
The hops should cover significant distance and height — explosive effort.
Continue for 20 to 50 yards.
Walk back to the start. Perform 4 to 8 sets.
Builds single-leg explosive power
Trains sprint mechanics
Develops cardiovascular conditioning
Carries over to running and athletic performance
No equipment needed
Excellent track-and-field warm-up

description.en: The lever seated leg curl is a single-joint isolation exercise performed on a seated leg curl machine. Sitting with the calves above a padded roller, you bend your knees to curl the weight downward by contracting the hamstrings. The seated position places the hamstrings under stretch at the top of each rep, which research suggests drives more growth than the lying or standing leg curl variations.

en: Sit on the seated leg curl machine and adjust the seat back so your knees align with the machine’s pivot point.
Adjust the ankle pad so it sits across the back of your lower legs, just above your heels.
Adjust the thigh pad to lock your legs in firmly. The pad should feel snug but not painful.
Grip the handles and sit upright with your back pressed against the pad. Brace your core.
Curl both legs down by bending at the knees. Keep your hips planted on the seat throughout.
Continue until your knees are fully bent or you reach a strong contraction in your hamstrings.
Squeeze your hamstrings hard for one second at the bottom.
Slowly extend your legs back up under control over two to three seconds. Feel the deep stretch in your hamstrings at the top.
Direct hamstring isolation with constant tension
The stretched (top) position drives more hamstring growth than the lying version
Allows safe, comfortable training to muscular failure
Easy to load progressively in small increments
Excellent finisher for posterior-chain workouts
Works the biceps femoris and semitendinosus directly

description.en: The side lunge stretch is a wide-stance standing stretch where you shift your weight to one bent leg while keeping the other leg straight. It deeply stretches the adductors (inner thigh) of the extended leg and provides a glute stretch on the bent leg side. It is dynamic, functional, and an excellent warm-up.

en: Stand with feet wider than shoulder-width apart, toes pointing forward.
Place your hands at your chest or on the floor in front for support.
Shift your weight to your right leg by bending your right knee and sitting back on that side.
Keep your left leg completely straight with the foot flat on the floor.
Lower your hips as low as comfortable. Feel the deep stretch through your left inner thigh.
Keep your chest up and back flat.
Hold for 20 to 30 seconds. Breathe deeply.
Shift to the opposite side and repeat.
Deeply stretches one adductor at a time
Combines hip and inner-thigh flexibility
Functional dynamic stretch
Excellent warm-up or cool-down
No equipment needed
Builds hip mobility for squats

description.en: The side lying outward knee kick, also known as a clamshell, lies on the side and lifts the top knee while the feet stay together. The motion isolates the glute medius and hip abductors.

en: Lie on your side with the knees bent at forty five degrees.
Stack the hips and shoulders in line.
Keep the feet together throughout the movement.
Brace the core and engage the glutes.
Lift the top knee away from the bottom knee.
Stop when the hips begin to rotate backward.
Squeeze the glute at the top of the rep.
Lower with control and repeat for all reps then switch sides.
Trains the glute medius and hip abductors.
Improves hip stability for running and lifting.
No equipment needed.
Excellent warm up before squats and deadlifts.
Carryover to single leg balance.
Reduces knee valgus on heavy squats.

description.en: The side-to-side box shuffle is an agility drill where you stand beside a low box or step and quickly shuffle your feet on and off the box laterally. It builds lateral foot speed, ankle stability, and cardiovascular conditioning. It is a popular drill in football, basketball, and soccer training.

en: Stand to the right of a low box, step, or platform (4 to 12 inches high).
Place your left foot on top of the box and your right foot on the floor to the right of the box.
Quickly switch — push off and place your right foot on top of the box and your left foot on the floor to the left of the box.
Continue alternating rapidly. Stay on the balls of your feet.
Pump your arms naturally for speed.
Keep your hips low and your body in a slight athletic stance.
Move as fast as you can while maintaining clean footwork.
Perform for 20 to 45 seconds per set.
Builds lateral foot speed and agility
Develops ankle stability
Excellent warm-up and conditioning drill
Improves change-of-direction speed
Easy to set up with any low surface
Raises heart rate quickly

description.en: The side twist is a seated rotational stretch where you sit cross-legged or with legs extended and twist your torso to one side. It stretches the obliques, lower back, and hip rotators while improving thoracic spine mobility. It is a simple, effective stretch for improving rotational flexibility.

en: Sit on the floor with legs crossed or extended in front of you.
Sit tall and lift your chest. Place your right hand behind your right hip.
Place your left hand on your right knee for leverage.
Inhale and lengthen your spine. Exhale and gently twist to the right.
Look over your right shoulder. Keep both sit bones grounded.
Hold for 20 to 30 seconds. Breathe deeply and deepen slightly with each exhale.
Release and twist to the left side.
Do not force the twist — let your breath guide the depth.
Stretches the obliques and lower back
Improves thoracic spine rotational mobility
Relieves tension from prolonged sitting
Calming and restorative
No equipment needed
Easy to integrate into any cool-down

description.en: The single-leg bench squat stands on one leg in front of a bench and squats down until you sit on the bench, then stands back up on one leg. The bench provides a consistent depth target and safety catch, making it an excellent pistol squat regression.

en: Stand on your right leg in front of a bench, facing away from it.
Extend your left leg forward.
Squat down on your right leg until your glutes touch the bench.
Lightly sit — do not fully relax.
Drive through your right foot to stand back up on one leg.
Complete reps, then switch legs.
Adjust bench height for difficulty — lower is harder.
Aim for 5 to 10 reps per leg.
Excellent pistol squat regression
Bench provides safety and consistent depth
Builds single-leg squat strength
Adjustable difficulty by bench height
No weights needed
Develops balance and control

description.en: The single leg glute bridge with external rotation is a glute focused bridge variation. Adding an external rotation of the off leg loads the glute medius and adds rotational stability work to the standard bridge.

en: Lie on the back with the knees bent and feet flat.
Lift one foot off the floor and rotate the knee out to the side.
Keep the other foot planted close to the glutes.
Place the arms at the sides palms down.
Brace the core and keep the chest up.
Drive through the planted foot to lift the hips.
Squeeze the working glute and side glute at the top.
Lower with control and continue for all reps then switch.
Isolates one glute.
External rotation loads the side glute.
Bodyweight move.
Useful for hip stability.
Builds the glute medius.

description.en: The Smith one leg deadlift is a single-leg Romanian deadlift performed on a Smith machine. The fixed bar path provides stability that the freestanding single-leg RDL lacks, letting you focus on the working leg without balance demands. It builds hamstring and glute strength with strong unilateral loading.

en: Set the Smith machine bar at hip level.
Stand in front of the bar and grip it with an overhand grip.
Unrack the bar and step back into your stance.
Stand on your right leg with your left foot lifted slightly behind you.
Brace your core and lift your chest.
Hinge at the right hip while extending your left leg back behind you.
Lower the bar along your right leg until you feel a strong hamstring stretch.
Drive your right heel into the floor to stand back up. Switch sides.
Builds single-leg hamstring strength
Fixed bar path provides stability
Reduces balance demands
Corrects left-right imbalances
Strong glute development
Useful for rehab or beginners

description.en: The square hop is a plyometric footwork drill where you hop in a square pattern — forward, lateral, backward, and lateral again — landing in each of four quadrants. It builds foot speed, ankle stability, and multi-directional plyometric power. It is a staple agility drill for sports.

en: Imagine a square on the floor about 1 to 2 feet wide. Stand in the lower-left quadrant.
Hop forward to the upper-left quadrant. Land softly on both feet.
Hop laterally to the right to the upper-right quadrant.
Hop backward to the lower-right quadrant.
Hop laterally to the left back to the starting lower-left quadrant. That completes one round of the square.
Continue for 5 to 10 rounds in one direction, then reverse direction for the same number.
Stay on the balls of your feet. Land softly with bent knees.
Use chalk, tape, or visualization to mark the square.
Builds multi-directional plyometric power
Develops ankle stability and foot speed
Improves coordination and timing
Excellent agility drill
No equipment needed
Cardiovascular conditioning

description.en: The stick overhead full sumo squat stretch is a mobility hold that combines a deep sumo squat with an overhead reach. The lifter sits in a deep wide squat holding a PVC pipe overhead. The combo opens the hips, adductors, and shoulders all at once.

en: Stand tall holding a PVC stick wider than shoulder width overhead.
Lock the arms straight and pull the stick apart for tension.
Set a wide stance with the toes pointed out at 45 degrees.
Brace your core and keep the chest tall.
Sit straight down into a deep sumo squat.
Drive the knees out wide and let the hips drop low.
Hold the deep squat with the stick locked overhead.
Stand back up to finish.
Strong hip mobility move
Stretches the adductors
Trains shoulder mobility
Useful warm-up
Builds full body coordination
Strong mobility hold

description.en: Strongman Fingals Fingers is a classic strongman event named after the rocks at the Giants Causeway. The athlete grabs the end of a long heavy pole on the ground and lifts and tips it up and over so it lands flat on the other side. The event tests posterior chain power.

en: Stand at the end of a long weighted pole on the ground.
Bend down and grip the pole near the end.
Brace your core hard and keep the back flat.
Drive through the legs to lift the pole.
Continue driving up to tip the pole vertical.
Push the pole past vertical to start it tipping over.
Step back as the pole falls forward.
Move on to the next pole. Continue for the working time.
Trains posterior chain power
Strong strongman event
Builds total body strength
Useful for strongman athletes
Builds explosive power
Trains grip and back

description.en: The suspended split squat is a Bulgarian split squat variation where the rear foot is elevated in a TRX strap or gymnastic ring. The suspension adds instability to the rear leg, increasing hip and ankle stability demands on the front leg.

en: Set a TRX strap to about mid-shin height. Stand facing away from the anchor.
Place your left foot in the foot cradle behind you.
Hop your right foot forward to a comfortable split stance position.
Hold dumbbells at your sides or bodyweight only.
Lower your left knee toward the floor by bending your right knee.
Descend until your right thigh is parallel or your left knee is just above the floor.
Drive through your right foot to stand back up.
Complete reps on one side, then switch.
Suspension adds instability to the rear leg
Increases hip and ankle stability demands
Builds single-leg strength
Exposes left-right imbalances
Useful when no bench is available for Bulgarian squats
Scalable with bodyweight or dumbbells

description.en: The suspension sumo squat is a wide-stance squat performed while gripping suspension straps for assistance. The wide stance emphasizes the glutes and adductors while the straps provide support that reduces the load on the legs. It is a strong stepping stone for working up to bodyweight wide squats.

en: Anchor suspension straps overhead at a sturdy point.
Stand facing the anchor and grip the handles with both hands.
Set your feet wider than shoulder-width with toes turned out.
Step back to create tension in the straps.
Brace your core and pull your shoulders back.
Squat down by bending your knees and pushing your hips back.
Use the straps as light support throughout the descent.
Continue down until your thighs are parallel to the floor or deeper. Drive up to standing.
Builds wide squat strength with assistance
Emphasizes glutes and adductors
Reduces balance demands
Stepping stone to bodyweight wide squats
Easy to scale by changing strap tension
Useful for rehab or beginner training

description.en: The Svend bench press is a lying bench press variation where you squeeze two weight plates together between your palms and press them up and down from your chest. The constant inward squeeze activates the inner chest fibers more than standard bench pressing.

en: Lie on a flat bench. Hold two light weight plates pressed together between your palms at your chest.
Squeeze the plates together hard with both palms — maintain this inward squeeze throughout.
Press the plates straight up from your chest to lockout.
Keep squeezing the plates together at the top.
Lower back to your chest under control. Maintain the squeeze.
The squeeze is more important than the weight.
Use light to moderate plates. Aim for 12 to 15 reps.
Focus on the inner chest squeeze throughout.
Activates the inner chest fibers
Constant inward squeeze targets pec adduction
No dumbbells or barbell needed — just plates
Builds chest mind-muscle connection
Excellent chest finisher
Unique pressing variation

description.en: Upward-Facing Dog (Urdhva Mukha Svanasana) is a foundational yoga backbend where you press up from a prone position with arms straight, hips off the floor, and weight on hands and the tops of feet. It is more demanding than Cobra Pose because the hips and thighs are lifted off the floor, requiring more strength and shoulder mobility.

en: Lie face down with legs extended and the tops of your feet pressing into the mat.
Place your hands on the floor under your shoulders, fingers pointing forward.
Inhale and press strongly through your hands and feet. Straighten your arms completely.
Lift your chest, hips, and thighs off the floor. Only the tops of your feet and your hands touch the floor.
Roll your shoulders back and down, away from your ears. Open your chest.
Engage your glutes, quads, and core to protect the lower back.
Gaze forward or slightly up — do not crank your head back.
Hold for 1 to 3 breaths. Transition to Downward-Facing Dog by exhaling and lifting hips back.
Deeply opens the chest and front shoulders
Strengthens the arms, wrists, and shoulders
Stretches the abdominals and hip flexors
Strengthens the spinal extensors
Foundational pose in vinyasa flows and Sun Salutations
Counteracts forward-hunched posture

description.en: The weighted hyperextension is a loaded version of the standard back extension, performed on a 45-degree hyperextension bench while holding a weight plate or dumbbell against the chest. Adding load progressively builds the lower back, glutes, and hamstrings far beyond what bodyweight reps can achieve. It is a staple accessory lift in powerlifting and strength programs.

en: Set up on a 45-degree hyperextension bench. Adjust the pad so it sits just below your hip bones, with your feet locked under the foot pads.
Hold a weight plate or dumbbell against your chest with both arms crossed over it.
Brace your core hard and lock in your back angle.
Start with your torso angled up so your body forms a roughly straight line from heels to head.
Hinge forward at the hips by lowering your torso toward the floor. Keep your back flat — do not round.
Lower until your torso is roughly perpendicular to the floor or until you feel a strong stretch in your hamstrings.
Reverse the movement by squeezing your glutes and hamstrings to bring your torso back up to the straight-line position.
Do not hyperextend (overarch) the lower back at the top. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Increase load progressively over time.
Allows progressive overload of the posterior chain
Builds the lower back, glutes, and hamstrings aggressively
Trains the hip-hinge pattern under load
Excellent accessory for deadlift and squat strength
Builds spinal erector endurance and capacity
Easy to scale up with progressively heavier loads

description.en: The wheel rollout with wall support uses a wall as a stopping point. The wall caps the range of motion so the lifter can build up to a full ab rollout safely.

en: Kneel on the floor a few feet from a wall.
Hold the ab wheel with both hands in front of you.
Brace the core and squeeze the glutes.
Roll the wheel forward keeping the arms straight.
Continue rolling until the wheel reaches the wall.
Hold the bottom position briefly with the body extended.
Use the abs to pull the wheel back to the start.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
Builds anterior core strength.
Wall stop limits range for safe progression.
Excellent foundation for full ab rollouts.
Trains anti extension through the core.
Carryover to plank and front lever progressions.
Develops total core stability.

description.en: The wide stance jump squat to narrow stance jump squat is a plyometric drill that switches stance widths between jumps. The wide stance recruits the inner thighs and glutes while the narrow stance hammers the quads.

en: Stand with your feet in a wide sumo stance with toes turned slightly out.
Lower into a deep squat keeping the chest tall.
Push through the floor and jump up explosively.
In midair, snap your feet together into a narrow stance.
Land softly with feet close together and bend the knees.
Sink into a narrow stance squat with the torso upright.
Jump up again and land with feet wide in the sumo position.
Continue alternating wide and narrow stance jumps for all reps.
Builds explosive power in the legs and hips.
Hits the inner thighs in the wide stance and the quads in the narrow stance.
Spikes the heart rate for excellent conditioning.
Improves landing mechanics and ankle stability.
Develops coordination through stance changes mid air.
Requires no equipment and can be done anywhere.
